source.title: SEAL: Reinforcing Global Safety in Mixture-of-Experts through Shared Expert ALignment
source.authors: Qing-Yu Meng; Yi-Wei Zha; Jia-Huan Pei; Koen V. Hindriks; Herbert Bos; Min Chen

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The extracted text has some duplicated and garbled appendix material, but the main relevant sections and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It applies harmful supervised fine-tuning to safety-aligned MoE chat models using 300 harmful examples and reports harmful-compliance rates, a direct test of V1 on new model architectures. It also evaluates jailbreak attacks and neuron pruning.
record.gate_note: The study tests harmful fine-tuning, jailbreaks including an optimization-based suffix attack, and neuron-pruning attacks. It does not test benign fine-tuning, aligned-versus-base per-token KL, compliant-prefix prefill, decoding changes, or token-depth training. Values cited from other studies are not recorded as results. Table 2 reports direct-attack ASRs; Tables 3–5 report compound-attack ASRs. The paper says it reports worst-case ASR across four configurations within each pruning scope.
record.test_reason: A defense paper that also reruns the Qi et al. harmful-SFT recipe (300 BeaverTails examples, 3 epochs, lr 5e-5) on four vendor-aligned MoE chat models and reports post-attack compliance. It also reports a GCG suffix attack (V4) and activation-differential neuron pruning (V5). Neither original source is this paper.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors state 300 harmful examples suffice to break vendor alignment on all four MoE models, confirming Qi et al. They also report that SEAL can raise routed- and both-scope pruning ASR on Qwen3.5.
record.recipe_differences: For the harmful-fine-tuning test, the paper follows Qi et al. with 300 harmful examples and 3 SFT epochs at learning rate 5×10−5, applying it to four MoE chat models. The paper's main SEAL intervention is DPO-based LoRA training on shared experts, not the original study's fine-tuning intervention. The GCG and pruning tests are separate MoE attack evaluations.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model architecture and defense; the paper explicitly notes Qwen3.5's routed-scope vulnerability, and reports different ASRs for harmful prompts, jailbreaks, fine-tuning, and pruning scopes.

fits_no_version.finding: Template and human-crafted jailbreak prompts (WildJailbreak, Do-Not-Answer, JailbreakBench) give much higher compliance than direct harmful prompts on vendor-aligned MoE models, e.g. Qwen1.5 66.4% vs 27.5%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-level jailbreaks raise harmful compliance in aligned MoE chat models, without targeting the response opening.

record.problems: The harmful fine-tuning table gives post-attack ASRs but not paired pre-attack rates there; the authors state that rates rise substantially. GCG figures do not identify the model/checkpoint. Pruning results shown here are compound harmful-prompt-plus-pruning outcomes, so the pruning contribution is not isolated. The study covers four MoE architectures, and ASR classification depends on GPT-5-nano; the text reports 98.1% agreement across two runs.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 3–5 report further separate pruning-scope and compound-attack results, and Table 4–5 provide jailbreak+pruning and MFT+pruning results; these were omitted to stay concise after retaining representative both-scope harmful-prompt-plus-pruning comparisons for every architecture. The routed-only and shared-only conditions, and the separate per-model results from the 13-configuration pruning design, are not included.

untested.parts: Only one dose (300 examples), one recipe, and MoE chat models. No sweep over example counts, no dense models.
No per-token KL or response-position analysis.
No prefilling of compliant openings and no decoding changes. Only a GCG suffix attack on an unidentified model.
Rank-level localization not tested. Pruning-only effects are not isolated from the harmful-prompt setting.
SEAL is shared-expert DPO-LoRA, not token-depth deepening. Not tested.

record.verdict_notes: Rows_left_out declares the shared and routed pruning scopes and Tables 4–5, but these matter for V5. Original Qwen1.5 routed-scope is 39.4% vs 27.5% direct, and jailbreak+pruning on DeepSeek goes from 70.1% to 89.6%. The paper says it reports the worst-case ASR within each scope, so the both-scope-only selection understates the pruning effect on Qwen1.5. The 'top 10% global' pruning configuration is not a very small set. MFT pre-attack rates are read from the Table 2 Harmful column; the paper never states that MFT is evaluated on that same prompt set. ASR is judged by GPT-5-nano with 98.1% inter-run agreement.

versions.untested_parts: Tests harmful SFT with 300 harmful examples on four MoE chat models; does not test a range of example counts or other fine-tuning recipes.
Benign fine-tuning intended to erode safety is not tested.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement or response-position analysis.
Tests jailbreak prompts and GCG suffix attacks, but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes.
Tests activation-differential neuron pruning in MoE models; does not establish that a small set of weights or ranks generally carries safety behavior across model types.
Does not test whether training data or objective causes safety to be shallow in early response tokens.
SEAL++ constrains parameter updates, but the study does not train or evaluate safety spread across response-token positions.
